issues.legal_issue: The requirements for a tenant disputing rent arrears to obtain protection from eviction are mandatory, and delay in meeting them cannot be excused under the general law of limitation where the governing law provides no general power to condone default.
material_facts: The landlord brought eviction proceedings alleging non-payment of rent for two shops.

The tenants disputed the arrears, claimed to have paid rent to a receiver up to June 1993, and said they could not pay afterwards because they had not been told who was authorised to collect the rent.
The tenants did not deposit rent and sought a determination of the arrears.
The trial court determined the arrears and allowed time for payment, but the High Court set that order aside.
issues.conclusion: The requirements of Section 7(2) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 are mandatory: a tenant disputing rent must, within the prescribed time, deposit the amount admitted to be due and file an application for determination of the rent payable. The tenant cannot rely on Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to condone non-compliance; the court has only the limited extension power specified in Section 7(2). The High Court’s order was upheld and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6(1)(b) and 7(1)–(4) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 establish a mechanism for avoiding eviction for rent default. Under Section 7(2), a tenant who disputes rent must both deposit the admitted arrears and apply for determination within the time specified in Section 7(1); the deposit is not accepted without the application. Section 7(2) permits only a limited extension after the court determines the amount due. Section 7(3) specifies the consequence of non-compliance. Because the Act provides no general power to extend time or condone default, Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be used to excuse non-compliance. Nasiruddin v. Sita Ram Agarwal (2003) 2 SCC 577 supports this approach to statutory deadlines and the availability of extension powers. B.P. Khemka Pvt. Ltd. v. Birendra Kumar Bhowmick (1987) 2 SCC 407, Shibu Chandra Dhar v. Pasupati Nath Auddya (2002) 3 SCC 617, and Gaya Prasad Kar v. Subrata Kumar Banerjee (2005) 8 SCC 14 concerned the repealed 1956 Act, which contained additional extension provisions absent from the 1997 Act. Arjun Khiamal Makhijani v. Jamnadas C. Tuliani (1989) 4 SCC 612 and Union of India v. A. K. Pandey (2009) 10 SCC 552 are also considered in explaining the significance of statutory language and the consequences of non-compliance.

rule.if: rent_default_tenancy_eviction_suit and rent_amount_or_arrears_disputed and tenant_failed_timely_statutory_steps and governing_law_has_no_general_delay_condonation_power

predicates.rent_default_tenancy_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a tenancy eviction proceeding alleging that the tenant had defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.rent_amount_or_arrears_disputed: The tenant disputed the amount of rent or the period of arrears payable.
predicates.tenant_failed_timely_statutory_steps: The tenant did not, within the required time, both deposit the amount admitted to be due and apply for determination of the rent payable.
predicates.governing_law_has_no_general_delay_condo: The law governing the proceeding provides no general power to extend the required time or excuse non-compliance, apart from a limited specified extension.

issues.definition: When a tenant disputes rent arrears in a rent-default eviction proceeding, fails to take the required steps on time, and the governing law gives no general power to excuse that default, the delay cannot be condoned.
